content: Congenital hypothyroidism (CHT) is a condition that affects approximately 1 in 3000 to 4000 newborns. It is one of the most common preventable causes of intellectual disabilities. Effective management of CHT requires early diagnosis and immediate treatment to prevent abnormal neurodevelopmental outcomes. A key issue in the treatment of CHT is determining the optimal initial dose of levothyroxine to ensure the best possible intellectual development. Currently, it is unclear whether a high dose of thyroid hormone replacement is more effective than a low dose in treating CHT. Further research is needed to establish the appropriate dose that optimizes mental and psychomotor developmental outcomes. The objective of this study was to compare the effects of high versus low doses of initial thyroid hormone replacement therapy in infants with CHT. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were identified through searches of The Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and reference lists of published studies. Only RCTs that investigated the effects of high versus low doses of initial thyroid hormone replacement for CHT were included in the analysis. The initial search yielded 1014 records, of which 13 publications were selected for further review. After screening the full texts of these 13 studies, only one study met the inclusion criteria. This study evaluated 47 infants with CHT and used the same cohort at two different time points to assess the effects of high versus low doses of thyroid hormone replacement. The study focused on two primary outcomes: the time required to achieve euthyroid status and neurodevelopmental outcomes. The study found that a high dose of thyroid hormone replacement was more effective in increasing serum thyroxine and free thyroxine levels to the target range and in achieving earlier normalization of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels compared to a low dose. Additionally, children who received the high dose demonstrated significantly higher full-scale intelligence quotient (IQ) scores compared to those who received the low dose. However, there were no significant differences between the two groups in terms of verbal IQ or performance IQ. The study did not report on growth outcomes or adverse effects. The authors concluded that there is currently only one RCT evaluating the effects of high versus low doses of initial thyroid hormone replacement for CHT. The available evidence is insufficient to definitively determine whether a high dose is more beneficial than a low dose in the treatment of CHT.
